utterances.text: Do you remember that you talked about the policemen leaving the police station and getting to Ismet Kuci's house? "Before they got to Ismet Kuci's house, that's when I saw them, but I believe they had left the police station previously, they had come out of the police station."

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I believe it; I saw them leaving the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan. I'm sorry. Carry on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, is it true you didn't actually see Bujar get killed, the moment he was killed?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still inside when I heard the crying, the shouting, and when I went outside, I saw Bujar lying down on the balcony and Flora, who was crying from the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that you did not see the moment Bujar was killed because you were in the house, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I just heard the noise and when I went out, I saw Bujar lying on the balcony and Flora shouting, Oh, they've killed Bujar, they've killed Bujar. But they killed them all. They just killed them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, I only want to know about what you actually saw. We need to draw a line between what you saw and what you heard. Other than that, I accept everything you say. But I do know exactly what is your direct personal knowledge and what is something that you heard from others. Therefore, we might as well move on.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put everything in my statements, everything that I saw and experienced, everything that I saw with my own eyes. It's not things that I heard because there was nothing to hear from other people. I saw these things with my own eyes, my own eyes. Everything I observed - my children, my husband, the women - I saw everything with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, you tell us today that you saw Zoran, and that you recognised him on the 26th of March, that morning. I'm putting it to you that you never in your life spoke to Zoran and that you don't know what he looks like.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never spoken to Zoran, but I do know him very well. I know him really well. I've seen him -- I saw him quite often with his wife in Suhareka. I regret to say it, but his wife was actually a friend of mine, and I hate myself for being so bitter. And we were at school together. We went to the same class of economics in school, and so I know Zoran very well. I used to see him very often in Suhareka with Slavica. And I really hate myself for these feelings that I have because she was a very nice Serb woman. My father was a friend of her father at that time. I know Zoran very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, you first said on the 4th of December, 2007, that you actually knew his wife and that was before a chamber of the war crimes tribunal, district tribunal, in Belgrade. You had never uttered that fact before; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true. I didn't want to mention that. I hate myself for having had her as a friend. I hate myself for having had her as a friend, and that's why I didn't want to mention that. But I do know Zoran very well. I saw him so often in Suhareka. Everyone knew him. He used to go out with the Albanians. He grew up with Albanian bread. He knew how to speak Albanian perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I think the moment has passed, Your Honours. I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, you gave evidence on the 15th of May, 1992 [sic]. You made a statement to the investigators. You said this: "What I remember is I heard a Serbian man shout in Albania, Bujar, where are you? I recognised the voice of that Serb man, and his name was Zoran. This was the man that Drilon and Sedat had been telling me about."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please wait before you answer. Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Learned counsel has referred to evidence given on the 15th of May, 1992. The events occurred in 1999. And if references are made to a statement, it would assist if we are informed what these statements are and the correct date, so that we are able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, it clearly can't be a statement in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certainly not. 1999. I may have misspoken myself or maybe it was misinterpreted. The statement to the investigator of the Hague Tribunal was given on the 15th of May, 1999, the one that I am quoting now. I do apologise to the interpreters if it was me who misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And can you give a paragraph or a page number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. The English reference is page 7, paragraph 5. [In English] Starting with "The next thing I remember I heard ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the point of the question, Ms. Berisha, I think was that in this statement in 1999, if you agree that you said that, what you said is that you recognised the voice of a Serb man who was calling or shouting in Albanian and you then said his name was Zoran. Is that something you said then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is the truth, and Drilon and Sedat saw him and Driloni spoke up and said, Dad, dad, that's Zoki, that fat guy; because the Albanians called him Zok, not Zoran. And then when we saw all the police outside, he shouted and I recognised it as Zoran's voice. It was actually Bujar, it was actually Bujar who was called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I would like to remind you that you stated before the Belgrade court that you had never spoken to Zoran; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I've never spoken to Zoran, but I know him. I know him very well, but I just never had an occasion to speak to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, counsel refers to a statement that was given to the Belgrade court. Could we have a reference to this statement and a paragraph number to assist us in following counsel's line of questioning, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did submit for translation all the relevant portions of the transcript dated the 4th of December, 2007, evidence given before the war crimes district tribunal in Belgrade; however, the translation has not been completed, not to any extent whatsoever, in fact. I will not be tendering this transcript. I'm merely asking the witness questions given the fact that she was there and that she answered certain questions there. I'm presenting the answers to her, and she can tell us whether that was indeed the case or not. As for my reference, the witness claims that she saw Zoran. She explained how exactly she saw him and when, whereas it is the Defence position that she never saw him at all. It was based on the stories that she heard and based on the voice that she thought she recognised that she could actually place him at the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there something further, Ms. Gopalan, from that response?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be helpful perhaps if counsel were to read out the section in the statement that he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With a reference for the transcript to the paragraph number, if you could, Mr. Djurdjic. It should be the same number whether in English or in Serbian or in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd be glad to oblige; however, the translation is not ready. As a result, I cannot quote the page or the paragraph. I did read directly from the transcript, though. In relation to the first quote, first of all, this is D0001, it's one of our exhibits, D0001-0347, which has not been translated yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You recognise, I'm sure, Mr. Djurdjic, that it becomes very difficult both for the Chamber, for the witness, and for the Prosecution to be able to follow and comprehend your questioning when it's based on a statement that none of us have, or a transcript that none of us have. The witness in particular may be at a significant disadvantage in having to try and remember, A, whether anything was said on the occasion you suggest, and if so, what precisely might have been said. You have put this question; we'll see whether the witness can answer. But I'm afraid the Chamber is going to have to limit your questioning of this type to the extent that it's going to be based on documents that are not before the Chamber and are not in e-court and are not available to the witness or anyone else here. But pursue this one question, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we introduced the Serbian transcript into the e-court system. Unfortunately, we have so far not been able to get a translation for it. That is why I never came up with the proposal of having this admitted. This was for the sake of a later translation. I'm just quoting from the transcript the relevant portions, Q and A. I want to hear the witness. I want to see what she has to tell me. Is this true or is this false? If she says it's false, fine, then let's move on. I entirely understand the difficult situation which I now find myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The emphasis you place on your question, "is it true or is it false," highlights the problem. The witness may have no idea unless and until she can see a transcript of what she said precisely what words she used at some other time. That is the problem. Now, we have suggested that you might pursue on this occasion this question that you've already put to see whether the witness remembers saying that or not. If she doesn't remember, it doesn't mean that it's false or true; it simply means she doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, madam. Do you remember that when prompted by the president, Ms. Birahi, the following question: "Mrs. Berisha, did you ever have occasion to speak to Zoran earlier on?" Answer: "No, no. I have never spoken to Zoran. I have only spoken to his wife. Zoran's wife was a childhood friend. I hate myself for that. I travelled to school during our secondary school with Zoran's wife many times ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, is it not true that you were never in contact or indeed spoke to Laza Vera, Vera Petkovic, Zoran's mother?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Vera his mother, no, but I used to see her quite often in the street, and I used to see how she spoke to other people. But personally, I never had occasion to talk to her. We called her Laza Vera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, will you agree with me if I put it to you that you had not even heard of her before the incident occurred that involved the OSCE vehicle, late in 1999, possibly early 1998 -- late in 1998, possibly early 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I had heard of her much earlier. I know her as a person. She was a large woman, and I used to see her quite often in town. That's not true, that I only learnt of her that year. No, no. I used to -- I knew of Vera. All the Albanians used to know her, even the Albanians in my village Mushtisht, because she had an Albanian friend there. I knew her earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you never spoke to her, did you? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true, I never talked to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, is it true, and I think this is something that you confirmed today, about the 26th of March, 1999, the policemen did not actually go into Vesel Berisha's house, did they?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police arrived to the house where we were, and they came into the yard. They did not go into the house. They shot with their arms, but I didn't see how they killed Bujar. I just heard the noise. And at that moment I heard shouting and they said, Get out of the house, out of the house; and so we left the house. They came to the house of Vesel Berisha but did not enter it. It was a very short period of time that we were inside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, I would like to ask you to stick to the substance of my question, please, when providing your answers. Is it not true that the policemen never told you in which direction to run when you left the house, Vesel Berisha's house?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just shouted at us in Serbian, Get away, go away, and cursed us, swore at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, my question was, is it not true that the policemen never told you in which direction to run, and in that case the answer is yes, that's true, they just shouted at us in Serbian. So the answer should be a yes, should it not?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what kind of answer you want. I'm telling you that the police came and shouted at us, told us to get out of the house; and we set off running towards our house. From Vjollca's house we ran towards our house. They did not direct us in a particular direction. They just shouted at us. It was total confusion at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You've explained everything now. Am I right if I say that outside the pizzeria you found other members of the Berisha family, and they didn't tell you how they came to be there, or why?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met other members of the Berisha family there, Hajdin's family and Avdiu's, and I asked them, Who told you to come here? And they said, The police told us to come here. And there was nothing else that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you would have pressed on, as simple as that, had you not found them there?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we would have done, we perhaps would have survived, all of us. What sort of question is that? What do you mean, what would we have done? I was taking care of all the children. I would have left. I ran, and when I saw Vjollca and Flora, Sebahate, I stopped to be with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Let me just ask you this: What about right across the street behind the municipality building? Is the house of your husband's uncle there?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's the house of Vesel Berisha, not of my husband's uncle. You're talking about the house of Jashar Berisha, who worked at the gas station?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no, Mrs. Shyhrete. The brother of your husband's father, he's the one I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brother of my husband's brother is Vesel Berisha. He is the father-in-law of Vjollca, and that house is behind our house. And that's where the two policemen came, and they killed Bujar and shouted at us and told us to leave. That is the house of the uncle, my husband's uncle. But there's another uncle and his house is in the centre of Suhareka. His name is Rasim Berisha. His house is not behind that one. It's in the centre of Suhareka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do apologise, but there was a person who presented himself as the brother of your husband's father. Would I be right in saying that you did not see a single member of the military on the 26th of March, 1999, in Suva Reka while this was going on?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, I saw movements of vehicles and buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You saw them moving along the road, along the street outside?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a column of vehicles, when I was on the street, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: A column of vehicles that was on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But that column, that convoy was on the road. It was moving, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you cannot say how many policemen were there in front of the pizzeria when you arrived and that you did not see a single policeman?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were talking about Lirija, when she called me, she said, Come over here, your uncle needs help. And she also called her other relatives over to help. Lirija's husband, she was pregnant, and she would have given birth two weeks later. And when Lirija and I were talking, I told her, I can't go over there. They'll kill me, too, and I have my children to take care of. Lirija started to move and help her people. By that time the police came and we were all forced into the pizzeria at that moment. I saw them with my own eyes; I'm not blind. I saw them. It all happened very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me then what sort of uniforms these policemen were wearing?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I'm not certain about the colour of the uniforms, but they were wearing uniforms, caps, and automatic rifles. But I'm not sure about the colour. A large group of them came, and Hava and Lirija were unable to go and help the men, so they remained there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Today you said that when passing by the petrol pump you met Jashar Berisha and that you spoke to him, and you told us about this conversation. Was there anybody else at the petrol pump besides Jashar Berisha at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a short moment in time. As we were running, he was -- he just asked me this, and I replied. I had no time to look around whether there was someone else. This is the moment when he asked me, What's going on, why are you running? And when I said to him that the Serbian police killed our men. He is the only person I spoke to at the petrol station. I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Shyhrete, do you remember when you testified before the war crimes department of the district court in Belgrade you were asked by Counsel Folic whether you could say whether the policemen who were in front of your house were also in front of the pizzeria: "Were these the same policemen who were in the witness's courtyard and in front of the pizzeria, did the witness recognise anyone," and then you answered: "I have said more than once, sir, that I couldn't see anyone in the pizzeria, whether they were policemen, civilians, or who these people were. I've stated that more than once."

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that I was unable to recognise who was who. There was a group of policemen, but I was amidst children and women; and I was unable to recognise them. But a group of policemen was there. In Belgrade they can write whatever they want, and they can change things. But I have explained what I went through to the investigators of The Hague and that is the truth about what the Serbian police did to my family, to the Berisha family, in Suhareka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Berisha, you received several very serious injuries. You were treated in several medical institutions. You must have voluminous medical documentation; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, in Kosova I was treated with basic medicine, and when I arrived in Albania the Italians in the Italian hospital performed an operation, and they removed part of the grenade. I don't know what it is called, but they removed it from my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hand over this medical documentation to the OTP? Did they ask for it?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that Rufus, the OSCE chief, who took me there to the Italian hospital, I think that he had the notes and the documents of what was removed from my body. But personally it was of no interest to me to get this documentation because rarely can someone understand my situation. This shrapnel in my body didn't mean anything at the time, and as I said, I still have shrapnels in my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Shyhrete, you misunderstood me. Did you give any medical documents to the Prosecutors of the Hague Tribunal, and did they ask you to give them that?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question very well. I understand you very well. And I told you that I did not get any document from the Italian doctors, and I did not hand over anything to the ICTY investigators in terms of documents. Had he asked me for documents, I would have asked Rufus for them, and I would have provided him with the documents. But these documents should be somewhere today. Personally, I didn't get any documents with me, but I know that the document exists and that the doctors, the Italian doctors, wrote down everything they did during the operation on those documents. It was a small hospital in Kukes where they performed operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention that we are getting concerned at the amount of time being taken. We had hoped to finish this witness, including re-examination, before the end of today and things have been moving very slowly during this last session. Could you please try and give attention to time as you look at your notes over the break. Thank you. We will adjourn now and resume at ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I hope that we can deal with the rest of the questions very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, do you remember on the 4th of December, 2007, you were in Belgrade appearing at the district court for war crimes. The previous morning there had been an ID parade, which is its formal name. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identification of those persons whose names I gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The identification of all persons accused before that chamber of the war crimes district court in Belgrade, all seven of them who you identified. There were seven groups. You were on the ground floor of that building at a quarter past 8.00 that morning when the ID parade began. Do you remember that? You were facing an investigating judge and then an ID parade took place.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave the names of only three persons. But the day their identification was made, and then after that we immediately went to court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, can you please answer my question? There were seven persons who were indicted before the war crimes district court in Belgrade, indicted for war crimes, regardless of how many you actually mentioned. You were shown seven groups with five persons each, and you were asked whether you could identify any persons who were in those groups. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have exhibit, Defence Exhibit D0001-3042. Your Honours, while we're waiting for the exhibit to come up, unfortunately, the first page was translated into English and then instead of page 2, page 4 was translated. This is an error because the page that we want to be looking at is page 2. However, this is page 1, the beginning of the record of the ID parade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My question: Do you remember that you failed to identify Zoran Petkovic during the actual parade?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. I couldn't recognise Zoran because he had changed a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please mark this for identification until such time as page 2 has been translated? By mistake, page 4 was translated instead of page 2, but the witness still confirmed what I asked her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification. I'm sorry, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I just confirm that the relevant page, which is page 1, is the document that's not available at the moment and that's the one that's being marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is being marked at the moment is a page 1 and a page 4, or alternatively it's the whole of the document in Serbian. Which was it that you had in mind, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked for the entire document to be translated; nevertheless, only page 1 has been translated, and the page that counts is page 2, containing the identification of Zoran Petkovic. We only have it in the Serbian. Soon we shall have a translation into English as well, and that relates to the entire document, or at least I hope so; and not only the relevant page, whereas page 1 has already been translated into the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will mark for identification the whole document in Serbian and the pages that have been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00023, MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Madam, is it true that you left Kosovo and Metohija at the Morina pass and you crossed the border into Albania?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Kosova and went to Albania through Kukes crossing. This is where I crossed, at Kukes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My apologies. And whose border crossing would that be?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, but I only remember that from Kosova, we went to Kukes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that when you crossed the border you failed to display any ID whatsoever? None of the documents were taken from you, were they?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any documents on me. I didn't have anything to give them, since I didn't have anything. I only had the wounds inflicted on me by the Serb police. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you have no certificate whatsoever showing that a blood sample was taken from you at the hospital in Albania following your surgery? No certificate by the Hague Tribunal OTP or, indeed, any other organisation that might have taken a sample of your blood.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get any certificates. I told you it was Rufus with me, the chief of the OSCE. I didn't get any -- any documents, any piece of paper. But the Italians operated me in their own hospital, removing the shrapnel from my stomach. It's true that I don't have any documents myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My last question, madam: Is it true that when you were in Bukosh you did not get off the tractor? You weren't at the school building. Everything you learned, you learned from other people. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn anything from others. I saw everything with my own eyes. I was on the tractor. I didn't get off the tractor. They didn't take me to the school, but from the tractor I followed up everything that happened. I didn't hear anything from other people. I didn't need to. I was one of them. I was in their midst.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In that case I have no choice but to show you your own statement dated the 15th of May, 1999. The English version is D0001-30 -- that's the Serbian. D0001-3010. Page 13 in the English, paragraph 3, starting with the following words: [In English] "The women were taken into the school and stripped down and their money and gold was taken, and they were released." [Interpretation] Have you heard this, madam? I can read the same thing back to you --

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The women said so, but they didn't take me to the school, nor did they ask me to get off the tractor. The other women were taken to the school, and these women told me that they were robbed of the money they had and the jewelry they had on them. I didn't see what they were robbed of at the school, this is true, but the other things I saw and I witnessed with my own eyes. I saw the Serb police shooting, I saw when they took away the young man along with the old man, and I saw that some of the young men never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I was only putting it to you that this was something you heard, you were not at the school building. Thank you, madam. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Gopalan, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: There is no re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder whether you can assist me, Ms. Berisha. You said during your questioning by Mr. Djurdjic that that morning you had heard a voice calling for Bujar in Albanian, and you recognised the voice as Zoran's voice. Do you remember the occasion we're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I would like to learn from you is how did you recognise Zoran's voice if you had never spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that it was Zoran because he spoke very good Albanian. It was Zoran. I didn't have an opportunity to speak to him, but I have run against him on the street with his wife many times. Therefore, I am certain that it was Zoran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because no one better than he, than Zoran, knew to speak such good Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it was the way that he spoke Albanian rather than the actual voice that caused you to identify the speaker as Zoran.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because his Albanian was -- you could take his Albanian for a native speaker's. I didn't say that it was Zoran's brother, even though his brother, too, was in the group. But in the case of Zoran, I am sure that it was him. It was his voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the -- Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on your questions, I have one final question, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll see first whether there is any question that Mr. Djurdjic would like to put arising from what I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did Miskovic also speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Miskovic. I am not sure about him, whether he spoke or not, Albanian. I knew Zoran more than him. But Miskovic's brother had a good company among Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Shyhrete, but he, too, spoke Albanian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Miskovic. I am not sure. But I do know about Zoran. I am 100 percent sure about his Albanian. He spoke Albanian every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that all Serbs in Suva Reka spoke Albanian if they needed to, just as you can speak the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Not all of them speak Albanian. We Albanians use -- most of us used to speak Serbian because we were obliged to learn Serbian in school, but this was not the case with the Serbs. Very few of them knew how to speak Albanian. Zoran was one of them. He spoke very good Albanian. And the brother of his wife, Kola, he too spoke very good Albanian. I know who spoke Albanian. We, all of us, knew how to speak Serbian, but the Serbs, there were a minority who spoke Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Madam Berisha, you just said that Zoran spoke very good Albanian. When was the first time in your life you ever heard Zoran's voice?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard Zoran speak many times when I met him with his wife. He spoke with Albanians; hey you, you are, where are you, and so on. But directly, I didn't have an occasion to speak with him myself, but I heard him speak Albanian many times with Albanians and with Serbs. It was Zoran. But in Belgrade in the court, in the district court, many years had passed, and he had changed a lot. He had become thinner. He was wearing glasses. So it was not the same man I used to know, whereas Miskovic and Zoran's brother I knew -- recognised him immediately. It is normal for me after nine years of what I went through that I was unable to recognise him. But when he spoke in the court, I immediately recognised Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Berisha. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Berisha, you'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions which are put to you in this matter. We would like to thank you for coming to The Hague. We know you've had to give evidence more than once, and it puts you under pressure. We appreciate your coming and we thank you for the assistance that you've been able to give. You may now go with the court officer and you are free to leave, to go back to your ordinary life. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next witness is Ali Gjogaj, and he will be taken by Mr. Matthias Neuner, who is just now coming in front of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is on the card now shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. I believe Mr. Neuner has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good evening, first of all.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: My name is Ali Gjogaj. I was born on the 25th of November, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, Mr. Gjogaj?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I'm a Roma.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what job did you perform in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: In the beginning, I worked as a cleaner in the city, in the town, and then in the meantime I was assigned by the civilian defence to work with corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us for which company did you work?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Public Hygiene, it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And who was your superior in Public Hygiene?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The director general was Jova Vujicic and Budimir Spasic was our director, supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I want to take you now to the events in 1999, the NATO air bombardments. Could you tell us what clothes was Mr. Jova Vujicic wearing during the air bombardment at work?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Jova Vujicic wore police clothes. He was a reservist wearing police clothes. He was a major by rank. This is -- this was his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And where was the headquarters of Public Hygiene in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: In the outskirts, on the road leading to Albania, this is where the offices were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could you tell us, during the NATO air campaign in 1999, who was having offices at the headquarters -- at the headquarters of Public Hygiene?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Different police that were there and that had come from Serbia were also stationed there, but I didn't know them. But there were other policemen there in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you're saying "in the office," where exactly were the police -- where exactly were the police from Serbia stationed? Can you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: They were stationed inside our company's building, in our offices. They removed our bosses, and they took over the offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. And why do you think these people coming from Serbia were policemen?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: They were wearing police uniforms, and you could tell from their uniforms that they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And when did these people start using offices in the headquarters of Public Hygiene?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: During the NATO air-strikes. They were not stationed there before, but in the meantime when the campaign started, the NATO campaign, a group of policemen came to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could you just, for the record, clarify in which town Public Hygiene was located?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Public Hygiene is situated in the western part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Of which town, please?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about your work which you performed during the NATO air bombardment. What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: I worked as a cleaner, but when the NATO air-strikes began, they provided us with civilian defence uniforms. And one day we were taken to Koris, to dig bodies. There they had prepared everything - the trucks, the bulldozers, everything. And I also worked at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there for a moment --

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: -- the Prizren morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You gave us a lot of information. You said, "One day we were taken to Koris." Could you first of all transcribe -- okay, the transcript says Koris. Could, you first of all, describe the location or the name of the location correctly, please.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Korisha, in fact, Lubizhda. I misspoke. It is a village, the village of Lubizhda, and the police had a check-point nearby; and they carried out their training, the army there. It was a training ground of the army of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: An army training ground for what?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The army practiced target practising, did target practising there in that training ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Would it help you if I show you a map that you could introduce us to where the training ground of the army called Korisa was?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We have prepared here hard copies. I know we're working with e-court system normally, but the point is that we had to combine two maps which are on separate sheets in e-court, and I'm referring here to item 65 ter number 615. And to make it also easier for this witness, we have produced print-outs today; and with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that these be distributed to the witness and please also to the Defence and the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We are making an attempt to do it electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, could I ask you maybe to wear your glasses as well, because it might not be very visible on the screen. We'll try it electronically first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For the record, in e-court it's uploaded, it's 65 ter number 615.01. Maybe to make it easier here we could not divide the screen but have the map on one screen, because it's very small, as it stands right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could the witness please have -- could we zoom out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. Could the usher please give the witness a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I would ask you to encircle, if you can, Korisa.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This is approximately the location where we dig out the bodies. It's not the exact location but the approximate area. It's very small on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark a 1 next to this area you just encircled.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. The first question I have for you is when approximately during the war did you go there?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: We went in early April. I'm not good with dates because we didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. And which year is that, sir? Early April which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell me who, if anybody, escorted you on your way there?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: They came to our houses to collect us. It was about 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. We were taken to the Hygiene Company. We were provided with clothes and gloves. Buda was there and three other men. And we straight set off in the direction of Suhareka and then returned to the training ground. There, everything was prepared, the excavators, the trucks, everything. Our director was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. Please try to answer my question. I only wanted to know who, if anybody, was escorting you on the way there. We will come to the rest later.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Buda and Jova, in other words, the director and my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And for clarification, these are the directors of Public Hygiene?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, the director of the Public Hygiene company, Jova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And once you arrived on the spot in Korisa, whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The police was there with another truck. We were in a van. We got off the van, and we were waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you describe the truck of the police. You say the police was there with a truck.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: It was a Pinzgauer, not a truck. There were four or five Pinzgauers of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Why do you believe these Pinzgauers were of the police?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Because it was known that police was present there, and the police moved about with these vehicles in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What colour did the vehicle have?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: It was dark, but to my recollection it was dark blue. They were police vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said already it was dark. What time approximately did you arrive in Korisa?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Around 9.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that the directors of your company were there, Buda and Jova. What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: The director Jova was wearing police clothes, while Jova [as interpreted] military clothes, army clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you said the police were there. What were the policemen doing on the spot in Korisa?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Some of the policemen were guarding us so that we wouldn't be disturbed, and some other policemen were removing bodies from another grave with an excavator on a different site.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many policemen were engaged in doing this removal of the bodies on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: About seven or eight policemen. Seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, could I direct your attention to page 41, lines 7 and 8. There seems an inconsistency of answer which you may need to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to clarify one issue. You gave an answer a moment ago about the clothes of the director Jova.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Jova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript reflects that you said, and it may be a translation error, that Jova was wearing police clothes and Jova was wearing military clothes. Could you clarify who from your directors was wearing which clothes, please.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Jova was wearing police clothes, the general director, while Budimir Spasic, who was our boss, immediate boss, he was wearing army clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. I could clarify this further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we maybe take a shot of this map for now. I will use it later on again, but I want to show an exhibit to make it really clear. Could I ask that this be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. We need also to receive the unmarked version first, and then the marked one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The unmarked version, Your Honours, is document ID 00615.01 will be assigned P00276.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could I kindly ask that the marked version be tendered as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just before the break, could I have 65 ter number 02375 be shown to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: While this is popping up, Mr. Gjogaj, I just wanted to follow up on your description of the uniforms of your directors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we enlarge this a little bit. I see my learned colleague on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is inappropriate to carry out identification or recognition of four uniforms shown to the witness. First of all, this sort of exhibit existed before when the witness participated in proceedings and this same picture was shown. If an identification is being carried out, and if the witness is meant to recognise something, there should be many more uniforms shown so that there really is a choice and the witness really does recognise something. But this is not recognition. Otherwise, you could show the witness a single uniform and ask him, Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Indeed, the Prosecution's aware that there are four options given here to this witness. The point is that these were the options initially shown to this witness when he was interviewed by investigators of this Tribunal, and in the Prosecution's submission, each of these four models here have a distinct character. So of course 10, 15 could have been shown as well; but we believe that still the witness has an option here to choose between one of the four models, or he could even say that his directors did not wear any of these four models. So he's at liberty to pick one of these options or even say, As far as I remember, the uniforms by my superiors, they are not reflected here at all, so in fact the witness has five choices. So we would submit that this is still a valuable choice for this witness to make. And the montage was also used in the previous case, in the Milutinovic case, and we don't have another montage prepared, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That answers the question I was about to ask: Is this the only prepared examples of camouflage uniform that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I was just asking again my colleagues. We don't have, I'm told, another such example with more options available. One moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What we can do ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would allow the question to be put, Mr. Djurdjic, recognising of course that the choice is limited, that the samples are not extensive; and that, therefore, there may be quite a question as to the weight which the Chamber in the end can give to the answer. But that will be something to be determined in due course. Mr. Neuner, we are over time. Do you want to press this issue now or should it continue tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I hope that we are getting a short answer tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very good. We'll press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, you talked about Jova Vujicic. Do you, in looking at this example, remember how eventually his uniform looked that night?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Jova's uniform was this one of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You will get a pen. If you could mark the sample you recognise with a 1.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. You have twice ticked this sample. It's the upper left-hand sample in the exhibit here. And do you recognise, if possible, any uniform which was Budimir Spasic wearing that night among the four samples?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Which one would that be? If you can mark it with a number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has marked the upper right-hand square on this exhibit. With this explanation, I would seek to tender it into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, we need to break for the evening now. We must now break to continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 in another courtroom. The people assisting you will show you where to go and give you further directions overnight. If you could be back here to continue your evidence tomorrow morning before 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now adjourn for the evening and resume at 9.00 in the morning, I believe it's Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.06 p.m.,
